q: Assembling a wine labelled simply Marlborough, a winemaker blends parcels off the valley floor with parcels grown south over the hills. What does each side bring?
opts: Ripe tropical weight from the Wairau, herbal cut and acidity from the Awatere
Oak character from the Wairau and stainless steel character from the Awatere
Colour from the Wairau and tannin from the Awatere
Sweetness from the Awatere and alcohol from the Wairau
exp: The regional name covers both valleys, so the blend is legal, and it is how most large-volume Marlborough Sauvignon is actually built. The two ripen a fortnight apart and taste like different wines, which is precisely what makes combining them worth the trouble.

q: Green capsicum, cut grass and blackcurrant leaf in a Sauvignon Blanc come from a family of compounds that sunlight and warmth break down. What are they?
exp: Pyrazines are present in the berry from early on and fall away as the fruit is exposed to sun and heat, so a cool shaded site keeps them and a hot exposed one does not. The Awatere retains far more of them than the warmer Wairau floor, which is most of why the two valleys smell so different.

q: Passionfruit, grapefruit and a boxwood note are absent from the juice and appear only once the ferment is running, because yeast cuts them free from odourless precursors. Which compounds are these?
exp: Thiols travel into the juice bound and inert, and how many are released depends on the yeast strain and on the handling of the fruit. Machine picking and a little time on skins raise the precursor load, which is one reason the Marlborough style holds together so consistently at enormous volume.

q: A winery chasing the classic Marlborough profile wants the aromatics unmasked and the acidity untouched. Which set of cellar decisions belongs to that aim?
opts: Cool fermentation in stainless steel, no malolactic, no oak
A month of fermentation on the skins, then ageing in buried clay
Fermentation halted with grape spirit, then bottling under cork
Warm fermentation in new oak, full malolactic conversion, two years in barrel
exp: Malolactic conversion would trade the wine's sharp malic acid for softer lactic acid and lay a dairy note over the fruit, and oak would simply cover the thiols the whole style rests on. Every choice in the recipe exists to get the vineyard's aromatics into bottle unaltered.

q: Harvesters work Marlborough's Sauvignon Blanc rows through the small hours with their headlights on. Beyond the machine's own convenience, what does picking in the dark protect?
opts: Night picking raises the sugar reading recorded at the weighbridge
Cold fruit ferments faster once crushed, which shortens the vintage
Cold fruit oxidises slowly, so the aromatics survive the wait for the press
Darkness stops pyrazines from forming in the berry overnight
exp: Warm juice browns and loses volatile compounds within hours, and a crop this size cannot all reach a press immediately. Fruit arriving at ten or twelve degrees rather than twenty-five buys the winery hours it would otherwise not have, and Marlborough now picks this way at a scale matched almost nowhere else.

q: Sancerre and Marlborough ferment the same variety, yet the New Zealand wine smells several times louder. Which difference in the growing season does most of that work?
opts: A long spell in new oak before the wine is released
A different grape entirely, sold under a borrowed name
Far heavier crops, which dilute the wine and exaggerate its aromatics
Fierce light over cold nights, building thiols and holding acid
exp: Sancerre ripens through a moderate continental summer and arrives flinty and restrained. Marlborough ripens under intense light with nights that drop away sharply, so it reaches tropical thiol ripeness without shedding either its pyrazine edge or its acidity, and the two wines have made one grape mean two quite different things.

q: Some producers ferment Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc with wild yeast in old barrels and leave it on its lees for a year. What are they trying to gain?
opts: The legal right to use the regional name on the label
Texture, savoury complexity and the ability to age
Residual sugar, since a barrel ferment always stops early
A higher alcohol level than the standard style can reach
exp: The mainstream style is bottled young, drunk young, and fading after two or three years. Lees ageing and old wood build a broader, more mineral wine that behaves more like white Bordeaux, and the price of it is the passionfruit rush that made the region's name in the first place.

q: Cross the Richmond Range westward out of Marlborough and you drop into a smaller, wetter region curled around a sheltered bay. Which region?
exp: Nelson sits on Tasman Bay and trades sunshine records with Marlborough, but it takes considerably more rain, so disease pressure and picking decisions matter more there. It is a region of many small producers making aromatic whites, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir rather than one of large volume.

q: Nelson splits between a flat plain of river gravels and a set of heavier clay hills that ripen later and give denser wine. What are the hills called?
exp: Moutere is old weathered clay-gravel and it holds water where the Waimea shingle drains it straight away, so the two halves of one small region ripen quite differently. The Wither Hills divide the Wairau from the Awatere in Marlborough, and the Teviotdale Hills shelter Waipara.

q: North of Christchurch a valley lies behind a low range that blocks the cold easterly off the sea, so it ripens warmer than the plains around it. Which valley?
exp: The Teviotdale Hills take the sea breeze out of the afternoon, and Waipara runs noticeably warmer than Christchurch at the same latitude. It lies inside the North Canterbury region, which is the name most labels now carry.

q: Limestone under parts of the Waipara Valley and a long dry autumn have made two grapes the district's calling card. Which pair?
exp: Waipara Riesling runs from bone dry to frankly sweet and holds a lime-and-honey line that rewards a decade in bottle. Its Pinot Noir is savoury and firm rather than plush, and both grapes depend on the long ripening period the shelter behind the hills makes possible.

q: Out on the flat shingle plains around Christchurch the wind comes straight off the Pacific and the season is short and cool. What does that ground favour?
opts: Full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot
Fortified wine matured for years in old wood
Lean whites and light-bodied Pinot Noir
exp: A short cool season leaves the whites sharply acidic and the reds light in body. The Canterbury Plains are gravel washed off the Alps, cold, exposed and quick to give up their heat, so a thick-skinned late-ripening variety will never finish there. The region's more serious wines come from Waipara to the north, where the shelter and the extra warmth change what is possible.

q: Vines in Central Otago push their roots into loess lying over a grey metamorphic rock that splits into glinting plates. Which rock?
exp: Otago schist formed under heat and pressure from old sea-floor sediment, and it fractures along its layers, so roots follow the cracks down to moisture. The loess above it is a fine wind-blown silt, and that pairing of a shallow fertile blanket over fractured rock is what growers there mean when they talk about their soils.

q: The coolest and highest of Central Otago's subdistricts sits in a river gorge, picks last of all and makes the most delicate Pinot Noir in the region. Which one?
exp: Gibbston is squeezed into the Kawarau gorge above the Cromwell basin and sits at around 320 to 420 metres, roughly a hundred metres above Bannockburn, so in a cold year the fruit barely arrives. When it does, the wine is perfumed and fine-boned rather than powerful, which is a style the rest of the region cannot easily copy.

q: North-facing slopes above Lake Dunstan catch more sun than anywhere else in Central Otago and give the region's richest, darkest Pinot Noir. Which subregion?
exp: South of the equator the north-facing slope is the sunny one, and Bendigo's terraces above the lake are the warmest ground in Central Otago. Gibbston is the coldest of the subdistricts and Wanaka sits apart to the north-west, beside its own lake rather than in the Cromwell basin.

q: Helicopters hover over Central Otago vineyards before dawn in spring, and wind machines turn all night beside them. Which hazard are the growers fighting?
exp: On a clear still night cold air pools on the valley floor while warmer air sits above it, and a machine or a helicopter simply mixes the two. An inland basin ringed by mountains delivers exactly those nights, and frost is the standing price Central Otago pays for its dry sunny days.
